name: Bezafibrate

lead: Bezafibrate is a long-established prescription drug for high triglycerides and mixed cholesterol problems. It comes up in fat-loss conversations because it activates the PPAR family of receptors, including PPAR-delta, the pathway behind compounds like GW501516 and linked to greater fat burning and a leaner body.

It acts mainly on PPAR-alpha, with some activity at PPAR-gamma and PPAR-delta, increasing triglyceride breakdown and altering HDL metabolism. Its trial record is in cardiovascular disease, dyslipidemia and the liver condition primary biliary cholangitis; no trials of fat loss or appearance outcomes were found.

paras: Its documented use is a prescribed oral tablet for blood lipids, taken under a doctor's supervision. In fat-loss forums posters mention it as a related PPAR option during cutting phases, alongside diet and training.

Reported effects include abnormal liver enzymes, muscle problems (rarely severe) and gastrointestinal upset. Sources list it as contraindicated in severe liver or kidney impairment, gallstone disease and pregnancy. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Bezafibrate is a lipid-lowering drug that acts on PPAR receptors, including the PPAR-delta pathway linked to greater fat burning and a leaner body composition. Fat-loss forums mention it as a relative of GW501516-type compounds. Its documented studies concern blood lipids and liver disease.

lead: Bezafibrate is an oral fibrate lipid-lowering drug sold under brand names such as Bezalip. It lowers LDL cholesterol and triglycerides and raises HDL cholesterol, and it is described as a pan-agonist of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), acting on alpha, gamma and delta subtypes.[1][2]

It is a prescription medicine, used mainly in dyslipidemia and, off the main labelled indication, studied in primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). It is mentioned in looksmaxxing and fat-loss discussions mainly as a PPAR agonist related to PPAR-delta compounds, though its documented uses are medical.[1]

paras: Bezafibrate is used for combined hyperlipidemia and hypertriglyceridemia.[1][2] In the Bezafibrate Infarction Prevention trial of more than 3,000 coronary patients with low HDL, the drug was tested for secondary prevention.[3] Encyclopedic sources report that its cardiovascular benefit appears mainly in patients with metabolic syndrome features, and that studies suggest it may delay progression to diabetes in people with impaired glucose tolerance.[1][2]

In primary biliary cholangitis, a placebo-controlled trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2018 examined bezafibrate added to standard therapy.[4] Further phase 3 trials registered in PBC and cholestatic itch were completed or listed as unknown status.[5][6][7]

Wikipedia reports that the main toxicity is liver-related enzyme abnormalities, with myopathy reported and rhabdomyolysis rare.[1] Grokipedia lists gastrointestinal upset and gallstone risk, with caution in renal impairment and combination with statins.[2]
Like other fibrates, bezafibrate activates PPAR-alpha, which increases lipoprotein lipase activity and triglyceride clearance; it also engages PPAR-gamma and PPAR-delta to varying degrees.[1][2]
Boehringer Mannheim introduced bezafibrate in 1977; it was patented in 1971 and approved for medical use in 1978 according to Wikipedia.[1]

Small trials have registered bezafibrate for mitochondrial myopathy, fatty acid oxidation defects, X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy and bipolar depression.[8][9][10][11] In mice with a human tau mutation it reduced tau hyperphosphorylation, per Wikipedia.[1]

Human trials have examined bezafibrate in coronary artery disease, dyslipidemia, primary biliary cholangitis and several rare metabolic conditions.[3][4][12][5][6][7][8][9][10][11] No studies found examining it for body-composition or appearance goals.
